content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published a position paper on mammography screening, which is part of a broader set of breast cancer guidelines to be developed in the coming years. These guidelines aim to address various aspects of breast cancer care, including prevention, diagnosis, treatment, rehabilitation, and palliative care. Currently, mammography screening is the only breast cancer screening method proven effective in organized, population-based programs. However, the reported benefits and harms of mammography screening vary significantly depending on the context, intensity of screening, and interpretation of available evidence. There is also uncertainty regarding the appropriate age groups for screening and the steps required to implement high-quality breast cancer screening programs. The primary objectives of the WHO guidelines are to provide policymakers, healthcare managers, and providers with clear, objective, and independent guidance on the balance of benefits and harms of mammography screening for women in different age groups. Additionally, the guidelines aim to disseminate recommendations to promote informed decision-making among policymakers, healthcare providers, women, and the general public. The guidelines focus on asymptomatic women at average risk for breast cancer in three age groups: 40–49 years, 50–69 years, and 70 years and older. Women with an elevated risk for breast cancer due to factors other than age are not included in the scope of these guidelines. The WHO emphasizes the importance of organized, population-based cancer screening programs, which target all at-risk populations in a specific geographical area. Key criteria for successful implementation include demonstrated feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and affordability of the screening process; coordination of activities by an autonomous management team; integration of cancer control planning into national health strategies; validated protocols for all steps in the screening process; adherence to evidence-based quality assurance guidelines; and sufficient organizational and financial resources to sustain the program. In well-resourced settings, WHO strongly recommends organized, population-based mammography screening for women aged 50–69 years, provided the healthcare system meets the necessary conditions for implementation and shared decision-making strategies are in place. A screening interval of two years is suggested. For women aged 40–49 years and 70–75 years, WHO suggests screening only in the context of rigorous research, monitoring, and evaluation, and if the necessary conditions for implementation are met. In limited-resource settings with relatively strong health systems, WHO conditionally recommends considering organized mammography screening for women aged 50–69 years, provided the healthcare system meets the necessary conditions and shared decision-making strategies are implemented. However, in settings with weak health systems, where most breast cancer cases are diagnosed at late stages and mammography screening is not cost-effective or feasible, the focus should be on early diagnosis. This involves ensuring universal access to prompt and effective diagnosis and treatment for women with symptomatic breast lesions. The WHO highlights that mammography screening can reduce breast cancer mortality by approximately 20% among women invited to screening programs. However, the balance between benefits and harms is narrow, particularly for younger and older women. There is also significant uncertainty regarding the magnitude of harms, such as overdiagnosis and overtreatment. Screening every two years appears to provide the best trade-off between benefits and harms. The guidelines stress the importance of access to objective, evidence-based information about the benefits and harms of breast cancer screening to enable women to make informed decisions. Cost-effectiveness analyses conducted by WHO and partners indicate that mammography screening is not cost-effective in lower-middle-income countries. In such settings, fragmented health systems and limited capacity may hinder the feasibility of nationwide screening programs. Regional programs may be an option in populations with a high burden of breast cancer, provided sufficient resources are available to implement and sustain organized screening programs. In resource-constrained settings, early diagnosis of breast cancer through improved public and professional awareness, prompt clinical assessment, and early referral of suspected cases is a highly appropriate and affordable strategy. This approach can complement screening strategies where they are justified, available, and feasible. Early detection and treatment of localized breast cancer can significantly improve survival rates, exceeding 80% in settings with accessible early detection and basic treatment services. In contrast, late-stage diagnosis in resource-limited settings results in five-year survival rates as low as 10–40%. The WHO position paper responds to the urgent need for guidance from member states, particularly upper-middle-income countries planning or implementing breast cancer screening programs.
